structure.title: Acts I–II · A father's condition reorganises a whole street
structure.text: Baptista announces that his younger daughter Bianca must wait until Katherina has a husband. Bianca's suitors suddenly have a shared interest in finding one. Petruchio arrives looking for a rich wife. Before he meets Katherina, men who want something from the arrangement have already supplied him with his description of her.

structure.title: Acts III–IV · At a lesson, at a wedding, at a dinner table
structure.text: Bianca's suitors use lessons in music and Latin to conduct a courtship under other people's noses. In the other household Petruchio uses a husband's authority to decide which meal is fit to eat and which dress is fit to wear. Shakespeare keeps changing houses so that we can see how much the freedom to play depends on who controls the room.

structure.title: Act V · An audience for a marriage
structure.text: The plots come together over a meal. The men devise a public comparison of their wives, with money riding on the outcome. The same words can do quite different work when spoken by a tired woman in private and by an accomplished speaker before a roomful of people with bets to settle.

people.name: Katherina and Bianca
people.role: Two sisters with a reputation apiece
people.text: Katherina is called difficult, Bianca sweet. Those judgments have helped determine who is wanted in marriage and under what terms. When the sisters speak to one another, they have years of rivalry and their father's preferences in the room with them.

people.name: Petruchio
people.role: A suitor who announces his method
people.text: He tells the audience how he means to interpret whatever Katherina says to him. Her sharpest reply can therefore be reported to her father as evidence of an understanding between them. His mastery of a story about their courtship precedes any mastery he claims over his wife.

context.title: Marriage negotiations give the jokes their stakes
context.text: A father can discuss a dowry with a prospective son-in-law before the household knows what the daughter thinks. Bianca's suitors need access to her father as well as to her. Their absurd disguises solve a real problem about who is entitled to make an offer and whose word will guarantee it.

notice.text: Listen to the name Petruchio insists on using.
notice.why: He shortens Katherina's name to Kate and invents a succession of flattering Kates around it. She has already told him what people call her. Before he has tried to govern a household he has tried, in public, to govern what she can be called.

notice.text: Watch what happens to a meal when Petruchio objects to it.
notice.why: The food is in the house. The person who needs it is present. A show of concern about its quality can separate the two just as effectively as a direct refusal. The comedy makes the machinery of the deprivation remarkably easy to see.

opening: Petruchio comes to Padua looking for a wealthy wife and hears of a woman everyone else considers impossible. Katherina refuses the sweetness expected of her, and he announces that he knows how to handle that. Their verbal sparring becomes a contest in which marriage gives one participant control over food, sleep, and the terms of reality. Shakespeare's comedy is funny, uncomfortable, and fiercely disputed because its central bargain is so exposed: what will a household do to obtain the appearance of a woman's willing obedience?
